blurb: A dense rosette of grey-green leaves that opens huge, sweetly fragrant white saucers in the late afternoon — each one fading to pink by the next morning and gone. Night-flying moths do the pollinating, and the show repeats all summer.
water: Low; xeric — well-drained ground, little or no supplemental water once established
seasons: Large fragrant white flowers ageing pink, opening late afternoon through summer; dense grey-green rosette
wildlife: Native bees and butterflies work the flowers

care.hardiness: CSU lists this as a Colorado native plantable to about 9,000 ft, so cold is not the constraint at Boulder's zone 5b–6a.[1]
care.planting: Plant in spring after the mid-May last frost, or in early fall, into ground prepared to suit it (see Soil). Set out young container plants — most of these natives resent having an established root system disturbed — and water them in well, then taper off.[1][2]
care.sun: Full sun, which is CSU's exposure rating for it.[1]
care.soil: Well-drained soil. It is a plant of dry slopes, gravelly flats and clay 'gumbo' banks — hence one of its names — so it will take heavy soil provided the surface drains and it is not irrigated.[1]
care.water: Low. CSU rates its moisture requirement low, and on the semi-arid Front Range that is the number that matters most — the commonest way to kill a xeric native here is kindness with the hose.[1][2]
care.spacing: Space to suit its mature spread of 12–18 in wide. A dense rosette of dark grey-green leaves whose fragrant flowers open in late afternoon and fade the next morning.[1]
care.propagation: By seed, which is how nearly all of these natives are raised and how they persist in a planting. Autumn sowing outdoors lets winter provide the chilling most of them want.[1]
care.bloom: Flowers roughly June through mid-August; CSU records the colour as white, pink and the height as 6–12 in tall.[1]
care.maintenance: Plan for it around the evening rather than the middle of the day: the flowers open in the late afternoon, scent the air after dark, and are finished by mid-morning. Site it by a patio or a path you use in the evening.[1]
care.troubles: Few pests or diseases when it is sited right. Crown and root rot in soil that stays wet is the usual cause of failure for a Colorado native in a Front Range garden, and it is a siting problem rather than bad luck.[1][2]

references.name: CSU Extension — Native Herbaceous Perennials for Colorado Landscapes (fact sheet 7.242, PDF: complete Table 1)
CSU Extension — Xeriscaping: Perennials and Annual Flowers (7.231)

edible.summary: No documented culinary use in the authorities consulted; grown as a fragrant native ornamental.[1]
edible.caution: No authority consulted documents a food use for white-tufted evening primrose, so this guide treats it as inedible — don't eat it. Other members of the genus have a food and oil record (notably *Oenothera biennis*), but that belongs to different species and this guide does not extend it here.[1]
